title: sleep
hook: a bird tied to a peg flies every direction, then lands where it's tied

segments.voice: Yesterday, sleep, and Charaka's three supports of life: food, sleep, and a disciplined way of living. Did you choose a bedtime on purpose, and keep it? Day one thousand three hundred fifteen.

A bird is tied to a peg by a long string. It takes off toward the trees and the string pulls it up short. It tries the other way, toward the roof. Short again. It tries every direction there is. Finally, worn out, it comes down and settles right at the peg, the one place it was tied all along. That picture comes from Uddalaka, the father we met over food, who taught his son with an ember. Now, in the very next part of the Chandogya Upanishad, he turns to his son and says: learn from me about sleep.
screen: `A BIRD ON A STRING.` → `EVERY DIRECTION, PULLED SHORT.` → `IT SETTLES AT THE PEG.`

segments.voice: Uddalaka starts with a word. The Sanskrit for he sleeps is svapiti. And the text plays on it, the way a teacher plays on a word to make it stick: svam apita, gone to his own. When a person sleeps, he says in paraphrase, he has gone home, united with sat, the Existent, being itself. That's why people say he sleeps: he has gone to his own. This is the Upanishad's own wordplay, a teacher's hook, not a dictionary entry. But look at what it does to the night. Sleep stops being a switch-off, a blank. It becomes a homecoming. Then the bird. Tied to a peg, it flies in every direction and finds no resting place anywhere else, so it settles where it's tied. In the same way, Uddalaka says, the mind flies in every direction, finds no resting place elsewhere, and settles down in the breath. For the mind, my dear, is tied to the breath. Look at what the picture holds. First, the day as flight. Messages, errands, worries, plans: the mind goes out and out, and it's meant to. The bird isn't scolded for flying. Second, the tether isn't a cage. It's what makes landing possible. Without the peg, there'd be nowhere to come down. Third, the tether is close. Not a mountain, not a temple far away. The breath, which has been going the whole time, under all the flying. And Uddalaka is only getting started. He is teaching his son what a self is, and sleep is one of his ways in. Every night, in his teaching, everyone takes the trip home, whether they notice or not.
screen: `SVAPITI: GONE TO HIS OWN` · `SLEEP AS A HOMECOMING` · `THE BIRD SETTLES AT ITS TETHER` · `THE MIND IS TIED TO THE BREATH`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let the bird fly, then let it land. Sit comfortably. For a little while, let the mind go wherever it likes: tomorrow, yesterday, a conversation, a list. Don't chase it back. Then notice the breath, still going under all of it, in and out. Each time the mind tires of a thought, let it come down there, on one breath, the way the bird comes down at the peg. Then let it fly again if it wants. If you pray, you can rest in prayer at the landing. The bell holds the time.
Sleep. In the Chandogya, svapiti, played on as gone to his own: a nightly homecoming, with the mind settling in the breath like a tethered bird. Today's word.
Your line: sleep. Tonight, when you lie down and the mind starts flying, don't fight it. Each time it tires, let it land on one breath. Day one thousand three hundred fifteen.

howItsDone: Some Vedanta teachers read Uddalaka's lesson on sleep as a hint about the self, and the tethered bird is used in teaching to show the mind coming to rest in the breath.

fork.setup: you're a bird tied to a peg by a long string. you've tried every direction and found nowhere to land. what do you do?
options: keep flying until the string snaps.
settle down at the peg you're tied to.

fork.reveal: it settles at its tether. so the mind, Uddalaka says, finding no rest elsewhere, settles in the breath.

original.note: Sanskrit: he sleeps. The Chandogya plays on it as svam apita, gone to his own.

trapdoor: what you thought: sleep is switching off.
what it means: in the Chandogya, the sleeper has gone home, to his own, and the mind settles in the breath like a tethered bird.
what a scholar hears: svapiti heard as svam apita, the text's own wordplay, inside Uddalaka's teaching on sat, the Existent.
